title: Batteries made from salt
voice: Every title, desc, comment or intro here is read by a player and is written as Envie speaking. See CLAUDE.md and _DESIGNS/envie-voice-and-text-rewrite-guide.md: plain short sentences, no em-dashes, European spelling, no emoji, facts and sources untouched. The optional 'envie' line on a slide is his own aside, one short sentence.

slides.text: What if the next big battery was made from salt?
slides.footer: I nearly laughed when I first read that. Then I kept reading.

slides.text: Almost every battery you own runs on lithium. Your phone, your laptop, most electric cars.
slides.footer: Lithium is brilliant. It is also rare, and its price can jump from about €17,500 to €60,000 a tonne.

slides.caption: And we need more batteries every year. They got 99% cheaper in 30 years. A battery that cost €100 back then costs about €1 now.

slides.text: So I looked one row down on the periodic table. Lithium has a sibling there. Sodium, the stuff in your salt.
slides.footer: Same family, same trick. Tiny charged bits rock back and forth between the two ends of the battery, like a rocking chair.
slides.envie: A rocking chair. I like that.

slides.caption: For every bucket of lithium in the ground, there are more than 1,000 buckets of sodium. In the sea, more than 60,000.
slides.envie: From up there, Earth is mostly sea. Plenty to go round.

slides.title: Same job, different ingredients
bad: About €17,500 a tonne of raw material
good: About €440 a tonne of raw material
Keeps about 90% of its power at -40°C

slides.text: So is lithium finished? Not at all. Sodium is heavier for the same energy.
slides.footer: An SUV on sodium alone goes about 350 km, Dublin to Cork with some to spare. On lithium, 400 to 600 km. Grand for city cars, scooters and buses.

slides.text: A battery beside a wind farm never moves. So weight does not matter.
slides.footer: What matters there is cheap, safe and long lasting. That is sodium's home ground.

slides.text: Wind and sun don't work to our timetable. Batteries save the extra for later.
slides.footer: Cheaper storage means less gas burnt to fill the gaps on a still winter evening.

slides.caption: Batteries that match wind and sun to when we use power could cut almost 15 billion tonnes of CO2 a year. That is about 280 times what all of Ireland emits in a year.
slides.bold: 280 times what all of Ireland emits
slides.envie: I had to read that number twice.

slides.title: Kinder to people and planet
bad: Cobalt, about 75% from Congo, where child labour in the mines is well documented
Millions of litres of water per tonne, taken from dry South American valleys
Shipped part charged, so a fire risk at sea
Dug up in a handful of countries
good: No cobalt or nickel in the cleanest versions
Made from salt and soda ash, far simpler to process
Ships fully empty, at 0 volts, so no fire risk at sea
Found almost everywhere, even in seawater

slides.caption: And it is not a lab idea any more. Factories making sodium batteries for the grid are set to grow 15 times, from 10 GWh in 2025 to 150 GWh by 2030.
slides.bold: not a lab idea any more
slides.footer: By 2030 that is enough each year for a home battery in every house in Ireland, eight times over. Over 95% of the new factories are in China, though.

slides.text: Plenty of home batteries here hang on a cold, damp outside wall. Sodium doesn't mind.
slides.footer: They keep working down to -20°C, colder than the coldest night Ireland has ever recorded. Finally, the Irish weather gets a win.

slides.text: Every big battery reaches Ireland by ship. One that can travel empty is safer.
slides.footer: Researchers in Limerick are building their own sodium battery, in a project called TRIDENT. And the first sodium home batteries have just reached the Irish market.

slides.text: So next time someone says batteries are too rare, too dirty or too dear, tell them about salt.
slides.footer: Sodium won't replace lithium. They will work side by side, each on the job it does best. More batteries, from stuff found everywhere, means more wind and sun on the grid.
slides.envie: I am properly excited about this one.
